item.title: Xi reiterates Mideast peace stance
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-25
Xi reiterates Mideast peace stance Two-state solution stressed in talks with Jordan's king President Xi Jinping reiterated on Monday China's position on the political settlement of the Middle East issue with the Palestinian question at its core, urging efforts to push for the resumption of talks between Palestine and Israel based on the two-state solution and the early establishment of an independent Palestinian state. Xi made the remarks during his talks with King of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan Abdullah II ibn Al Hussein in Beijing. The Jordanian monarch was on a weeklong state visit to China, which concluded on Monday. Xi emphasized that China has consistently advocated a comprehensive ceasefire, cessation of hostilities and the resolution of disputes through political and diplomatic means, and it maintains that the sovereignty and security of countries in the region, including Jordan, should be respected. Noting that the principle of "the Palestinians governing Palestine" must be upheld, Xi said that Palestine is the home of all Palestinians, and this principle should be implemented in advancing the governance of the West Bank and postwar reconstruction of Gaza. He underlined the need to adhere to humanitarianism, with the international community, especially the United Nations Security Council, taking responsibility for protecting the safety of civilians, ensuring humanitarian aid and preventing humanitarian disasters. Xi called for upholding fairness and justice, following international law, addressing both symptoms and root causes, and taking pragmatic actions to achieve a comprehensive, just and lasting solution to the Palestinian question at an early date. China values Jordan's unique and important role in the region and firmly supports it in safeguarding its national sovereignty, security and development interests, he added. King Abdullah II expressed Jordan's high appreciation for China's fair stance on the Middle East issue as well as its support for the just cause of the Arab states, saying that China's just position is very important to countries in the region. Jordan is willing to maintain close communication with China and continue to make positive efforts to ease the current situation to enable the people of Middle East countries to enjoy peace and prosperity. Regarding bilateral ties, Xi said that since the establishment of diplomatic relations between China and Jordan, both countries have consistently respected each other, treated each other as equals, and engaged in mutually beneficial cooperation, setting a vivid example of win-win cooperation and mutual learning between small and big countries with different social systems. In the face of international and regional situations of turmoil and transformation, building a more substantial and dynamic China-Jordan relationship meets the common expectations of the two peoples and aligns with the trend of solidarity and self-strengthening among countries of the Global South, he said. Xi called on both countries to promote their traditional friendship, enhance strategic mutual trust, deepen mutually beneficial cooperation, strengthen multilateral coordination, and push for greater development of the China-Jordan strategic partnership to make positive contributions to regional peace, stability and prosperity. China is willing to engage with Jordan at all levels of government, political parties, legislative bodies and local exchanges, and to strengthen the exchange of governance experiences, he said. Saying that the nature of China-Jordan cooperation is of mutual benefit and win-win, Xi underlined the need for both sides to further deepen the alignment of their development strategies, strengthen cooperation in traditional fields such as economy and trade, infrastructure construction, transportation and minerals, and expand new growth areas of partnership in the digital economy, artificial intelligence and green energy. China is willing to work with Jordan to implement the four global initiatives, strengthen coordination and cooperation in multilateral institutions such as the UN, jointly uphold an international system with the UN at its core and an international order governed by international law, and promote the building of a community with a shared future for humanity, he said. King Abdullah II said China is a great country that has achieved remarkable and admirable development accomplishments under the leadership of President Xi. Jordan firmly adheres to the one-China policy, recognizing Taiwan as part of the Chinese territory, he said. Noting that Jordan highly values its relationship with China, he expressed his country's commitment to deepening cooperation and exchanges with China in areas such as economy and trade, manufacturing, agriculture, science and technology, medicine, culture and education. He said that Jordan welcomes more investments from Chinese enterprises to achieve common development and prosperity. Jordan highly appreciates the four global initiatives proposed by President Xi and looks forward to China playing a more significant leadership role on the world stage, he added. Following their talks, the two leaders jointly witnessed the signing of multiple cooperation documents in fields such as diplomacy, economy and trade, supply chains and the judiciary. The two sides issued a joint statement on deepening the China-Jordan strategic partnership. Before the talks, Xi held a welcoming ceremony for King Abdullah II at the Great Hall of the People. caodesheng@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: A recipe for peace
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-25
French filmmaker and critic Francois Truffaut once said, "Every film about war ends up being pro-war" — a famous line that has been cited repeatedly, often by those who argue that war films inevitably glorify combat and turn violence into spectacle. This paradox has inspired creators to seek new narrative approaches for anti-war storytelling. This summer, a Chinese blockbuster is offering just such a response: a fresh perspective on war, seen through the eyes of a Chinese chef. Once Upon a Time in the Middle East, starring A-list actor Shen Teng as the chef, has become one of this year's most popular blockbusters. Since its debut on Aug 11, the film has grossed more than 1.6 billion yuan ($237.9 million), topping China's single-day box office charts for 14 consecutive days. It currently holds a rating of 8.6 out of 10 on the popular review aggregator Douban, with many Chinese moviegoers praising its nuanced portrayal of human complexity amid war and its thought-provoking reflection on the longing for peace. The third feature directed by Wen Muye, best known for his 2018 hit Dying to Survive, the film has an unusual premise in China's huge domestic market. Although the country has produced many war-themed films and television series over the past decades, few have combined overseas warfare with Chinese cuisine. For thousands of years, food in China has been far more than a way to satisfy hunger. It carries memories of family and home, reflects the diversity of regional cultures, and preserves traditions passed down through generations. These themes run throughout the film, which unfolds through the memories of its protagonist, Xu Fu, taking audiences back to 2002. Xu, a chef with 30 years of experience, leaves his elderly mother and teenage daughter behind in northeastern China to work at a restaurant in a Middle Eastern country, hoping to pay off his debts. At the farewell dinner, he and his mother eat dumplings, a traditional Chinese culinary gesture in some parts of the country. Families customarily serve dumplings when seeing someone off and noodles when welcoming them home, symbolizing blessings and hopes for those traveling far from home. Upon landing on foreign soil, Xu quickly showcases his exceptional culinary skills at the Loong (Dragon) Restaurant, owned by a local official with the country's water and electricity authority. Among the dishes he prepares is "loong tide top" (dragon raises its head), a mandarin fish scored along the back and deep-fried so that it curves upward, which symbolizes rising fortunes and a bright future. At first, everything indeed looks up. Xu's cooking quickly attracts local diners, and he becomes friends with Ma Junsheng, the restaurant's Chinese front-desk manager. But a sudden outbreak of war plunges the Middle Eastern country into turmoil, trapping the two men amid ruins and gunfire. From there, one tense twist follows another. Xu decides not to return home after his boss makes him an irresistible offer to stay. Then, following an unexpected bombing meant to kill both American soldiers and locals, Xu and Ma are arrested and treated as suspects. Their fortunes take a sharp turn for the worse, and they soon become entangled with a group of orphans' fate — teenagers and children who are being brainwashed by extremist militants that are themselves rejected by the local population. Yet even as the story moves deeper into the chaos of war, the film repeatedly returns to food as a symbol of connection and harmony. For Wen, that symbolism is rooted in his own cultural background. As a native of Changchun in Northeast China's Jilin province, Wen tells China Daily that he believes Chinese cuisine conveys a deeper message: a yearning for wholeness and harmony. "When Chinese families dine together, they traditionally gather around a round table, and chopsticks are used in pairs," Wen says, referring to the symbolism of pairs as a representation of reunion. "So, in China, the act of eating together carries the symbolic meaning of 'ceasing conflict'," Wen adds, revealing that he hopes the movie will help audiences discover that even amid struggles and sorrow, ordinary people hold on to the humble wish of sharing a good meal. The idea for the film dates back to 2017, when Wen was working on post-production for Dying to Survive, a film about an unlikely hero who smuggles medicine. "I read a news story about several Chinese people who ran restaurants in the Middle East and encountered war. It impressed me and gave me the impetus to create this story," Wen recalls. Several years later, the director began preparing for the movie, traveling to Jordan and visiting refugee camps, where he spoke with people who had lived through war. But due to complicated international tensions at the time, he chose to cast Egyptian actors, including then 13-year-old Omar Sherif and veteran Sherif Sobhy, who play an orphan and the owner of the Loong Restaurant, respectively. Sherif, whose great-grandfather was from Shandong province, learned Mandarin and about Chinese cuisine in Egypt for three months to prepare for the role. Additionally, Faruk Muhammad, a young Egyptian actor who also plays an orphan, impressed Wen during his audition. For his character — a boy exploited by an extremist armed group to become a suicide bomber — Muhammad made a backpack filled with handmade "explosive" props himself, as featured in the script he was given. "In the Arabic-speaking world, Egypt has a developed film and TV industry, as evidenced by its long-running Cairo International Film Festival, so we held casting calls there, and many actors showed up to audition," Wen says. But the majority of the production was completed in China. Some exotic landscapes and creatures, however, could only be captured abroad. "For instance, we shot a scene of dromedaries (one-humped camels) running across the desert. In China, Bactrian camels — the two-humped variety — are a more common sight," Wen says. To make the food scenes convincing, the production also brought in veteran chefs to coach the actors in cooking techniques and help design the dishes featured in the film. One of the most mouth-watering sequences shows Xu and Ma, assisted by more than 20 local orphans, preparing a wedding feast. The centerpiece is a large iron wok measuring more than 2 meters in diameter, turning the preparation of a celebratory meal into a striking visual spectacle. Speaking of the wok used to prepare a fusion dish that combines iron-pot stew, a typical cooking method in northeastern China, with Arabic-style grilled fish, Wen says the scene was intended to reflect the exchange and fusion of Chinese and foreign cultures through vibrant, everyday imagery. More importantly, it highlights the shared aspiration of people from different countries for a better life. "I'm not really a foodie, and I'm not much of a cook either. But what I want this film to say is, 'Eat well'. In China, those two words can carry much more meaning than they seem to. They hint at 'Take care of yourself'," says Wen. "In times of chaos, it can be a quiet expression of love — a wish that you stay safe, keep going, and above all, make it home," he adds.

item.title: China's large cruise ship taking shape
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-25
China's large cruise ship taking shape Adora Flora City, nation's 2nd home-built vessel of its kind, nearing 99% completion Construction of China's second domestically built large cruise ship, Adora Flora City, is nearing completion, with 99 percent of the work done, a project leader said. Wei Shengsheng, head of cruise ship programs at vessel maker Shanghai Waigaoqiao Shipbuilding, said on Friday that the cruise ship has achieved several key milestones, including dry-dock block erection, full hull integration, in-dock floating and undocking, and a sea trial in May this year. The vessel is currently in its final stage of completion, with various interior areas being handed over to the shipowner progressively. The fully ready ship is scheduled to be delivered to the shipowner and operator, Adora Cruises, on Nov 6, Wei revealed. "Over the next two months or so, our engineers and construction workers will complete the handover work of all systems and sections on board, support the classification and statutory inspections, and assist the shipowner in training crew members to familiarize them with the operation of various facilities and equipment," he said. Shanghai Waigaoqiao Shipbuilding is a subsidiary of China State Shipbuilding Corp, and a major construction contractor for the nation's domestically built large cruise ships. Wang Jingjing, a senior researcher at Luoyang Ship Material Research Institute, another CSSC subsidiary, said that in order to support the construction of large cruise ships and address the industry's long-standing reliance on imports for core materials, her institute has set up a joint team with Shanghai Waigaoqiao Shipbuilding to develop essential coating materials for cruise ships. Leveraging the institute's established capabilities in materials research and development, performance testing and shipboard adaptation, the researchers focused on four core products required for cruise ship construction: decorative coatings, flooring primers and adhesives, and epoxy deck coatings. "Our products are both flame-retardant and environmentally friendly. They can resist aging despite frequent cleaning and withstand corrosion from various substances," she said. According to Wang, the breakthrough has enabled the vessel maker to break free from dependence on imported key consumables during construction, effectively reducing overall building costs, shortening material supply cycles and filling gaps in China's high-end cruise ship supply chain. Adora Flora City is the second vessel to emerge from China's decade-long endeavor to independently build large cruise ships, which are recognized as the most difficult and sophisticated among all types of civilian ships to design and construct. Construction of Adora Flora City began in August 2022. At the peak of construction, around 4,000 workers were aboard the vessel every day. For the sea trial, a team of 937 engineering and technical personnel from 12 countries was on board to check the performance of all systems. Compared with the first domestically built large cruise ship, Adora Magic City, the second vessel boasts an optimized design and a larger size. Measuring 341 meters in length, Adora Flora City is 17.4 meters longer than Adora Magic City. It weighs 141,900 metric tons — about 6,400 tons more than the first ship. The new cruise ship also has 19 additional guest rooms, bringing the total to 2,130 rooms that can accommodate a maximum of 5,232 passengers. Its public areas are also larger than those on the first ship. Once put into service, the vessel will adopt Guangzhou, the capital of Guangdong province, as its home port. Guangzhou is also known as the "Flower City" due to its year-round spring-like weather and mild climate, which are ideal for flower cultivation. zhaolei@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Beat the heat with a cool addition to your wardrobe
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-25
Summer is nearly over, but the heat hasn't loosened its grip. As the last of the season's hot days linger on, the battle against high temperatures has moved beyond sunscreen and iced drinks. For campers trekking mountain trails, cyclists logging long rides and anglers spending hours under the sun, a new piece of wearable technology is drawing attention: the cooling vest. "It's like wearing a small electric fan inside your clothes," said an outdoor enthusiast surnamed Luo, who shared his experience on Chinese lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, or RedNote, after wearing one while cycling and camping. "As long as it's below about 35 C, it works surprisingly well. It's not an air conditioner, but when you're moving around in this furnace-like weather, even a constant breeze makes a huge difference." His experience reflects a growing market for wearable cooling technologies, as hotter summers fuel demand for products that allow people to stay outdoors longer — whether for work or recreation. The trend is emerging alongside the country's booming outdoor economy. Since 2019, participation in hiking, camping, cycling, trail running and fishing has surged. Chris Sheng, founder of outdoor gear retailer Nomad Union, said, "In Zhejiang province, where our company is based, outdoor activities are almost suspended for nearly two months every summer because of the heat. "These cooling vests borrow technology originally developed for industrial workers and adapt it for outdoor recreation, making summer activities much more comfortable." For manufacturers, wearable cooling equipment is becoming a fast-growing niche at the intersection of outdoor gear, consumer electronics and climate adaptation. One of the latest entrants is outdoor gear maker Esguard, based in Pinghu, Zhejiang province, one of China's largest outdoor apparel manufacturing hubs. Esguard has developed a cooling vest that combines ventilation with semiconductor cooling technology, lowering the wearer's perceived temperature by 8 to 15 C, the company said. Unlike conventional fan vests that simply circulate ambient air, Esguard's design integrates two semiconductor cooling modules with dual fans mounted on the back of the garment. Air is drawn into the vest, cooled by the modules and then circulated around the body, delivering what the company calls an "air-conditioned" effect. Powered by a 20,000 mAh battery pack, the vest can operate for up to 12 hours on its lowest setting, making it suitable for a full working day or extended outdoor trips. "We wanted to move beyond simply blowing hot air around," said Fang Xiaodong, general manager of Esguard. "The goal was to create a wearable cooling system that people can genuinely rely on outdoors." The company began developing the product in March after anticipating rising global demand for heat relief technologies. Working with university researchers, it has already begun exporting the vests to markets including Dubai, Saudi Arabia, Japan and South Korea. The technology is also finding a growing customer base among front-line workers. In Nanjing, Jiangsu province, where summer temperatures frequently exceed 35 C, sanitation workers were among the first to test the vests. Since mid-July, more than 20 cooling vests have been deployed across the city. The city's urban management authorities have since recommended wider adoption, with six districts planning to procure the equipment. "It's much more comfortable," sanitation worker Zhu Wenxian told Workers' Daily. "I'm sweating much less, and I don't feel as irritable after working outside." Another sanitation worker, Liu Fali, said the airflow has made long shifts noticeably easier. "My back stays dry now," he said, lifting the back of his vest to show the built-in fans. "I'm even drinking two fewer bottles of water a day." Delivery companies are also embracing the technology. In Xuchang, Henan province, local franchisees of ZTO Express have equipped more than 100 couriers with cooling vests to help them cope with the summer of prolonged extreme heat. One courier, who delivers nearly 300 parcels a day during the peak season, told Workers' Daily that the vest has made long hours on the road significantly more bearable.

item.title: Alibaba seeks HK$80 billion placement
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-25
Alibaba seeks HK$80 billion placement Raising equity gives firm longer-term funding; sends vote of confidence Alibaba Group is seeking to raise about HK$80 billion ($10.2 billion) through a new share placement in Hong Kong, which, if completed, would become the world's third-largest primary follow-on offering this year, behind only those placed by Alphabet and Intel. The placement, announced on Sunday, would mark Alibaba's first new share sale since its Hong Kong listing in 2019. More striking is where every dollar raised is headed — the company plans to use 100 percent of its net proceeds to strengthen its artificial intelligence capabilities, including expanding and upgrading AI infrastructure. Several sources close to the matter told China Daily that the offering was oversubscribed within an hour of its launch. One source close to the company disclosed that sovereign wealth funds and some long-term institutional investors showed keen interest. Right after the move, Alibaba's Chairman Cai Chongxin and CEO Wu Yongming bought a combined about HK$120 million of Alibaba shares. Guo Tao, deputy director of China Electronic Commerce Expert Service Center, said: "Alibaba's placement also has benchmark significance for China's AI industry. Alibaba's continued expansion in AI capital spending could accelerate development across China's domestic AI supply chain, from AI chip adaptation and intelligent computing centers to liquid-cooling systems." As the AI race shifts from a technology contest into a "capital endurance race", raising equity gives Alibaba longer-term funding while sending a vote of confidence through the broader sector, Guo said. The aggressive spending comes as AI emerges as an increasingly important growth engine for Alibaba. The company reported revenue of 268.95 billion yuan ($37.5 billion) for its fiscal first quarter ended June 30, with net profit attributable to shareholders of 10.54 billion yuan. Alibaba CEO Wu Yongming told analysts after the earnings release that annualized recurring revenue from AI-related products was expected to approach $10 billion in the next quarter. AI-related product ARR had already surpassed 49.5 billion yuan in the first quarter, Wu said. Jiang Han, a senior researcher at market consultancy Pangoal, said: "Alibaba's organizational restructuring was effectively designed to build a vertically integrated, full-stack AI operation, lowering transaction costs and speeding the deployment of new technologies. The improvement in commercialization returns mentioned by Wu is a direct monetization of that full-stack capability." Jiang added that Alibaba's AI investment was beginning to move from simply "burning cash" toward generating its own financial returns. Alibaba's fundraising also comes as the AI sector's capital requirements are ballooning globally, pushing companies to seek ever larger pools of financing. Anthropic confidentially filed for a United States' initial public offering in June and could list as early as October, with a targeted valuation of as much as $2 trillion. OpenAI is also targeting a potential fourth-quarter listing, while its valuation in private markets stands at around $850 billion. Alibaba's HK$80 billion placement puts China's largest tech firms squarely into that global capital race. But raising more money does not remove the biggest uncertainty hanging over the AI boom — whether commercial returns can keep pace with the extraordinary amount of investment. Investors are already showing some caution. Alibaba's US-listed shares closed at $119.34 on Monday, down 8.57 percent, while its Hong Kong-listed shares ended at HK$112, down 8.54 percent. "The biggest risk investors need to watch is not that AI fails, but that the pace of AI commercialization fails to keep up with capital spending. In the end, this competition will not be about who spends the most. It will be about who can make returns on AI investment exceed the cost of capital first," Jiang added. chengyu@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Lights, camera, tractors!
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-25
During the recent summer vacation, visitors followed local villagers along ancient lanes in Yinan county, Shandong province, joining a "supply team" bound for the front line. The immersive Retrace the Frontline Supply Route performance in Changshanzhuang village was not staged in a theater. Instead, it took place in the same locations locals once hauled supplies along to support frontline troops during the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression (1931-45). Since its launch in October 2024, the performance has drawn tens of thousands of visitors. "This is completely different from anything we've done before," said Sun Fangchao, a tourist from Jiangsu province. "I think he'll be thrilled about this for a very long time," he said while watching his 11-year-old son who moved along with the performance troupe. For the show's creators, that emotional response is the point of its unique staging. Yinan county is famous for the Yimeng Spirit forged by ordinary villagers who risked their lives to support the Communist forces through extraordinary sacrifice during the war against Japanese aggression and the War of Liberation (1946-49). The county has over 20 immersive Yimeng Spirit-themed performances, turning cultural tourism from a sightseeing experience into participatory education, according to the local government. The performers are villagers who know the heroic stories very well. Ma Junling, 35, became a performer this year. Before then, she had worked as a tour guide in her village, explaining the Yimeng Spirit to visitors. "Our village often receives groups of students on study tours. They are young and have limited understanding. A simple lecture couldn't hold their attention, but the live performances bring the stories to life and help children better understand the history and culture," Ma said. Changshanzhuang is far from an isolated case. Across Shandong, grassroots cultural creativity is flourishing through immersive performances, verses composed by farmers, and rural micro-dramas filmed on mobile phones. Ordinary farmers are picking up pens, smartphones, and scripts, becoming poets, actors and dramatists.

item.title: HK, Macao key gateways to the world
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-25
HK, Macao key gateways to the world Cities are ideal testing grounds for products on way to overseas markets For an autonomous driving company, moving a vehicle from a left-hand-drive market to a right-hand-drive city is not just a matter of shifting the steering wheel. The work involves developing the system from the ground up, with everything from product definition and the vehicle platform to the autonomous-driving system and human-machine interface redesigned around the traffic rules, road conditions and user habits of right-hand-drive markets, according to Guangzhou, Guangdong province-based autonomous driving technology company WeRide. That is why WeRide's new right-hand-drive Robotaxi project began in Hong Kong. "Few cities offer a tougher real-world test for autonomous vehicles than Hong Kong, where dense roads, mixed traffic and a mature public transport system converge in one of the world's busiest right-hand-drive markets," said Tony Han, founder and CEO of WeRide. The autonomous driving developer recently announced that it is working with vehicle maker Geely Farizon and local transport operator Kwoon Chung Bus Holdings on a mass-produced model designed around Hong Kong regulations, road conditions and operating requirements. Han added that if the vehicle works in the city's dense traffic, the experience can support its expansion into other key right-hand-drive markets including Singapore, the United Kingdom, Japan and Australia. WeRide is not alone in assigning Hong Kong a specific role in a wider innovation chain. For a growing group of Chinese mainland technology companies, Hong Kong and Macao are where products encounter new operating conditions, local partners and international capital before entering overseas markets. China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30) calls for faster progress toward high-level technological self-reliance and again supports Hong Kong as an international innovation and technology center. Hong Kong is also preparing its first five-year plan, where technological development is expected to play a pivotal role. Technological self-reliance, however, does not mean geographic self-sufficiency. An algorithm developed in a Beijing laboratory may need to be engineered, financed, tested against different rules and sold into markets with different languages and business practices, just as the emerging Beijing-Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao network connects those stages. "Hong Kong and Macao boast diversified international business environments, leading innovation resources and mature global trade and financial systems," said Huang Heping, general manager of international business development at Beijing-based space company GalaxySpace. "They are important gateways for mainland companies to connect with the global technology frontier, participate in international scientific cooperation and share China's innovation achievements," Huang said. GalaxySpace develops communications payloads, satellite platforms and related systems and has built capacity for lower-cost, large-scale satellite production. In early 2025, it established a low-Earth orbit broadband demonstration station in Hong Kong, followed by a connected-car trial project, placing a mainland-developed satellite system in a local transport setting with Hong Kong researchers. "Just as travelers need a power adapter when they go abroad, mainland space products need a 'converter' to enter international markets," Huang said. "Hong Kong is that crucial platform." For GalaxySpace, the next steps include further tests, research cooperation and applications that can be assessed by local partners. "We believe Hong Kong and Macao will connect the mainland aerospace industry chain with the global market and create considerable value for the global space industry," Huang said. Beijing Zhongke WengeAI Science and Technology Co is using Hong Kong in a different part of the same process. Founded in 2017 by artificial intelligence scientists from the Institute of Automation of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, the company specializing in AI-assisted decision-making went public on the Hong Kong bourse in June under the exchange's specialist technology company regime. In a bid to provide further support for high-potential specialist technology companies in their pre-commercial or commercial stages, Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited, also known as HKEX, launched a listing framework under Chapter 18C of the Main Board Listing Rules in March 2023 to allow such companies in frontier sectors to list without meeting traditional profit or heavy revenue requirements. As of June 30, 21 specialist technology companies had been listed under the framework, raising a combined HK$38.74 billion ($4.94 billion) through their initial public offerings, according to data compiled by RyanBen Capital. Thirteen of them listed in the first half, raising HK$29.82 billion. "What attracts us most to Hong Kong is its international business environment and its unique role as a bridge between the mainland and international financing markets," said Wang Lei, chairman of Wenge AI. Wang said the company hopes its Hong Kong listing will broaden access to international capital, providing sustained support for core technology development, AI product upgrades and expansion into new application scenarios. Its Hong Kong operation has also put it in contact with about a dozen overseas customers so far and allowed its products to be demonstrated in local financial settings, which can provide valuable feedback on compliance language, data formats and professional workflows, he said. Macao offers a multilingual route into another group of markets. Pachira, an AI speech recognition, analysis and synthesis company, has placed core research and talent in Beijing, its Chinese mainland headquarters, and operating functions in Hengqin, an island district of Zhuhai in Guangdong, adjacent to Macao, and its international operations center in Macao. "With Hengqin serving as the main base for commercialization, technologies refined in Beijing can be adapted to a wider range of applications and replicated at scale," said Ho Kuok Tou, founder and CEO of the company. "Macao, meanwhile, provides a natural testing ground for our international expansion — its concentration of hotels, tourism and leisure businesses, and cross-border financial services allows AI products to sharpen their multilingual capabilities and readiness for global markets," Ho added. To navigate Macao's multilingual environment and distinctive customer-service habits, Pachira has carried out localized iterations of its proprietary speech large language model. The resulting AI voice system, developed for local electricity supplier CEM, now handles high-volume billing inquiries, marking Macao's first use of an LLM in a customer-service system. The company said it plans to use its Macao operation to pursue opportunities in Portuguese-speaking markets, initially targeting smart-energy and cross-border financial applications in Brazil, as well as factory-installed automotive systems and overseas banking operations in Portugal. lijiaying@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Robot on the line
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-25
Robot on the line China's massive parcel logistics industry embraces tech in race for efficiency At a busy parcel sorting center in Guangzhou, Guangdong province, a humanoid robot works alongside human colleagues on a sorting line, repeatedly picking up packages and feeding them into the system. On a large screen overlooking the floor, its output is displayed directly against performance figures for human workers. It does not tire, but for now, it remains slower and far more expensive than an experienced human operator. Eight of these humanoid units have undergone trial runs at the center since March, capable of feeding as many as 1,200 parcels an hour into the sorting system, said He Yong, deputy director of China Post's Jianggao mail processing center. Yet while eye-catching, the machines represent a technology still in its rough experimental phase — a high-tech snapshot of the transformation unfolding across China's logistics landscape. By 2030, annual express delivery volume is expected to reach 270 billion items, according to the country's postal industry development plan for the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30) period. After decades of explosive, volume-driven growth powered by the expansion of e-commerce, China's express delivery sector has reached a structural turning point. Volume is no longer the metric that matters most. Handling over 100 billion parcels in the first half of the year alone, logistics giants can no longer survive simply by adding handling capacity, and so have shifted their focus to operational efficiency and unit-cost reduction. Companies are increasingly turning to artificial intelligence, robotics, autonomous vehicles and digital management systems to improve the efficiency and resilience of one of the world's largest logistics networks.

item.title: Every small effort matters for China-US friendship
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
Every small effort matters for China-US friendship Share - WeChat
Twenty-seven years later, American Ronald Sakolsky returned to Ordos, China's Inner Mongolia, to reunite with Yin Yuzhen, who transformed his donation into a vast forest. Sharing memories over fresh fruit, Sakolsky said that China-US friendship needs more people to take action. "Even a small amount can become a forest," he added.
